title: Γαλῆ καὶ ῥίνη
part: The Weasel and the File (Chambry 77 · Perry 59)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 77 (= Perry 59). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γαλῆ εἰσελθοῦσα εἰς χαλκέως ἐργαστήριον τὴν ἐκεῖ κειμένην ῥίνην περιέλειχε.
sentences.tr: Galē eiselthousa eis chalkeōs ergastērion tēn ekei keimenēn rhinēn perieleiche.
sentences.l: A weasel, having entered into a smith's workshop, licked all over the file lying there.
sentences.n: χαλκεύς is properly a worker in bronze, and by extension any smith. ῥίνη is the file or rasp; an initial rho always carries the rough breathing, which is why it is written ῥ and romanized rh. περιέλειχε keeps its prefix's force: she licked it round and round.

sentences.t: Συνέβη δέ, ἐκτριβομένης τῆς γλώσσης, πολὺ αἷμα φέρεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Synebē de, ektribomenēs tēs glōssēs, poly haima pheresthai.
sentences.l: And it came about, her tongue being worn away, that much blood flowed.
sentences.n: συνέβη with the infinitive is impersonal: 'it happened that…'. The genitive absolute ἐκτριβομένης τῆς γλώσσης is present, so the wearing-away goes on while the blood flows.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἐτέρπετο ὑπονοοῦσά τι τοῦ σιδήρου ἀφαιρεῖσθαι, μέχρι παντελῶς ἀπέβαλε τὴν γλῶσσαν.
sentences.tr: Hē de eterpeto hyponoousa ti tou sidērou aphaireisthai, mechri pantelōs apebale tēn glōssan.
sentences.l: But she was delighted, supposing that she was taking away something of the iron, until she completely lost her tongue.
sentences.i: She was pleased, imagining she was getting some of the iron off, until she had lost her tongue altogether.
sentences.n: τι τοῦ σιδήρου is a partitive genitive, 'some part of the iron'. ὑπονοέω, 'to suspect, to guess underneath', takes the infinitive of what is supposed. The blood is her own; the Greek leaves the reader to see that, and never says it.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος εἴρηται πρὸς τοὺς ἐν φιλονεικίαις ἑαυτοὺς καταβλάπτοντας.
sentences.tr: Ho logos eirētai pros tous en philoneikiais heautous katablaptontas.
sentences.l: The story has been spoken against those who in quarrels do harm to themselves.
sentences.i: The story is aimed at those who injure themselves in their quarrels.
sentences.n: εἴρηται is the perfect passive belonging to λέγω, 'has been spoken'; πρός with the accusative here is 'directed against'. Chambry prints φιλονεικία, from νεῖκος 'strife' — contentiousness, quarrelling for its own sake. Ancient copyists confuse it with φιλονικία, 'love of victory'; the two senses run together, and either fits the weasel.
